**Saturday, June 23, 1956**

The year you arrived in was cracking at its foundations in ways that wouldn't be fully visible until autumn. Four months before your birth, Nikita Khrushchev had delivered his "Secret Speech" to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party — a brutal denunciation of Stalin's crimes, the cult of personality, the purges, the terror. Copies leaked. The communist world shuddered. By October 1956, Hungary would be in open revolt, and Soviet tanks would roll in to crush it. By November, Britain and France would be humiliated at Suez. The postwar order that had seemed stable was revealing itself as provisional. You were born into the last months before that order visibly broke.

---

**The birthday you share**

Alan Turing was born on June 23, 1912 — forty-four years before you, to the day. He formalized the concept of computation before anyone had built a working computer. He broke the Enigma cipher during the Second World War in ways that shortened it by an estimated two years. He was prosecuted by the British government in 1952 for homosexuality, subjected to chemical castration as an alternative to prison, and died on June 7, 1954 — two years before your birth, on what would have been his forty-second birthday. The British government issued a formal pardon in 2013 — sixty-one years after his conviction, fifty-nine years after his death.

The connection runs deeper than the shared date. Turing spent his life working on problems whose full consequences he couldn't see. The computer revolution he made theoretically possible was just beginning when he died. The artificial intelligence he wrote about as a thought experiment in 1950 has, within your lifetime, become something that can hold a conversation, write prose, and generate images. You arrived two years after Turing, and you have watched nearly the entire arc of what he started.

---

**Sixteen years before your birth, to the day**

On June 23, 1940, Adolf Hitler made his only visit to Paris. He had conquered it three days earlier. He arrived before dawn with a small group — Albert Speer, the sculptor Arno Breker, a few others — and toured the sleeping city for about three hours: the Opéra, the Eiffel Tower, the Invalides and Napoleon's tomb, Sacré-Cœur. He was back in his car before most Parisians woke up. It was the single morning of his life he spent in Paris, in a city he had just seized and would hold for four more years.

Sixteen years later, on the same date, you were born into a world in which that occupation was history. France was free, rebuilding, entering its own postwar boom. The man who stood under the Eiffel Tower at dawn on June 23, 1940 had been dead for eleven years.

---

**Six days after you were born**

On June 29, 1956, President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act into law. It was one of the largest public works projects in American history: 41,000 miles of interstate highway connecting the country coast to coast, financed by a new federal fuel tax, conceived partly as a military necessity and transformed almost immediately into the backbone of American civilian life. It rewired where people lived, which cities grew, how goods moved, what a family vacation looked like. You were less than a week old when the physical landscape of the country you would grow up in was committed to concrete.

---

**The world during your first months**

You were born during the Montgomery Bus Boycott. Rosa Parks had been arrested the previous December; the boycott that followed had been running for seven months when you arrived, and it wouldn't end until December 1956, when the Supreme Court ruled Alabama's bus segregation laws unconstitutional. For the entire first half-year of your life, the Black community of Montgomery, Alabama was walking to work rather than submit to the system as it stood. You came home from the hospital to a country where that was happening — quietly, determinedly, at the cost of significant hardship.

Meanwhile, Elvis Presley had released "Heartbreak Hotel" in January and watched it go to number one. "Don't Be Cruel" and "Hound Dog" followed in July. His Ed Sullivan appearance came in September 1956, seen by sixty million people. Rock and roll existed before your birth but became the dominant cultural force of your childhood in the months immediately following it.

---

**Your sixteenth birthday**

On June 23, 1972, the day you turned sixteen, President Nixon signed Title IX of the Education Amendments into law. No person shall be excluded from participation in any education program receiving federal funding on the basis of sex. The transformation that followed was generational: women's athletic programs, professional schools that had quietly capped enrollment, workplaces that drew from the universities — all of it shifted over the decade following that signature. The generation of women entering college in the late 1970s entered a different institution than their mothers had found. It happened on your birthday.

---

**The arc**

You are 70 years old. You were born before Sputnik, before the first American in space, before the birth control pill, before the Beatles recorded their first album. You were thirteen when humans walked on the Moon. Thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell. Forty-five on September 11, 2001. Fifty-one when the iPhone was introduced. You have now watched Turing's thought experiments about machine intelligence become, within a single human lifetime, something that holds conversations and writes prose.

The Suez Crisis that was building when you were born ended in humiliation for Britain and France and marked the real end of European imperial power. The Hungary that Soviet tanks rolled into when you were four months old is now a member of NATO and the European Union. The Montgomery Bus Boycott that ran through your first six months of life led, within a decade, to the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act.

The typewriter — a machine patented on your birthday's date in 1868 — is gone. The computing machines that replaced it trace their lineage directly to the man who shared your birthday and died before you were born.

Seventy years. Almost none of it was predictable from the morning of June 23, 1956.
